dedupe_keys.name: leeds teaching hospital 12 month prospective evaluation of isolation room capacity and isolation failures

description: This case study measures whether a large hospital had enough single rooms to isolate patients with transmissible infections. Neil Wigglesworth and Mark H. Wilcox of Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust and the University of Leeds, England, published it in the Journal of Hospital Infection in 2006. They followed every infection control request for isolation in an 1,100-bed teaching hospital for 12 months, ran four point-prevalence surveys of single room use, and related isolation failures to the incidence of new clinical MRSA isolates by ward. The article is available online by subscription, and the abstract is free on PubMed. Coverage is one hospital. Caveats: results reflect one hospital's ward layout and infection mix in the mid-2000s, and the data are not published. There were 845 isolation requirements, of which 185 (22 percent) could not be met; three quarters were for MRSA or Clostridium difficile, failure rates ranged from 0 to 57 percent by specialty, only 12 to 19 percent of single rooms were used for infection control, and failures correlated with MRSA incidence, while wards with at least 30 percent single rooms almost never failed. Simulation uses: isolation demand, failure rates and single room ratios for hospital capacity and outbreak surge models. Related records: the CDC healthcare-associated infection progress data (data-cdc-nhsn-hai-progress-report-data) give national infection indicators.
